title: Browsers, CORS, and Preflight Requests
learning_outcomes: Explain how browsers, cors, and preflight requests affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from same-origin policy to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on browsers, cors, and preflight requests in web networking and http fundamentals. You will connect same-origin policy to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Browsers, CORS, and Preflight Requests matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying same-origin policy deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: HTTP is the application-layer request/response protocol; message semantics live in methods, status codes, and headers. In this lesson, treat “Browsers, CORS, and Preflight Requests” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Browsers, CORS, and Preflight Requests

content_blocks.expected_output: The example shows a request target and headers followed by a response status, metadata, and JSON representation. example.test is illustrative and is not a live service.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Same-origin policy”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Cross-Origin Resource Sharing” and “CORS versus authentication and authorization”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Inspect the complete request and response before diagnosing an API failure. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating browsers, cors, and preflight requests. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Same-origin policy” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Browsers, CORS, and Preflight Requests with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating browsers, cors, and preflight requests as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: HTTP is the application-layer request/response protocol; message semantics live in methods, status codes, and headers.
